sources.text: After its sometime allies were ousted in elections in Hungary and Serbia, Moscow has seized on Poland’s constitutional standoff in its effort to weaken Europe’s support for Ukraine.

sources.headline: Polish PM Donald Tusk urges president to confirm judges amid constitutional crisis
sources.text:
Published on 2 November 2026 - 17:16 GMT+1•Updated
18:32
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has called on President Karol Nawrocki to confirm judges elected by parliament to Poland's Constitutional Tribunal.
The move comes after protesters and riot police faced off outside the court last week following the suspension of its president, in the latest incident in an intensifying stand-off over judicial appointments and control of the Tribunal.
"Resolving the conflict is simple and can be achieved without amending the constitution," Tusk wrote in a post on social media on Monday. "The President recognises the judges lawfully elected by the Sejm, as stipulated by the constitution, and they take up their duties at the Tribunal."
He also accused Nawrocki of "opting for a forceful confrontation, which could cost Poland dearly."
Since returning to power in 2023, Tusk has vowed to resolve the constitutional crisis, which has been going on for more than a decade.
The nationalist opposition retains control of the constitutional court, and while parliament has elected new judges, not all have been allowed to swear an oath before the president. Appointments to the Tribunal have become highly politicised, with some querying its independence.
The previous PiS government appointed politically committed judges to the court in 2015, who are recognised neither by Tusk nor the European Union.
The crisis escalated on Friday night when police deployed around the Tribunal as judicial and political authorities took steps affecting its leadership. Nawrocki cut short a trip from Senegal to return to Warsaw as the situation unfolded.
Conservative demonstrators and members of Poland's right-wing and far-right opposition branded the government's moves as a "coup d'etat," while the pro-European ruling coalition said the actions were necessary to preserving the rule of law.
On Saturday, Nawrocki held talks with political leaders, but these produced no major results.
The European Commission has said it is closely monitoring the crisis and that the Polish Parliament had the right to appoint judges to the constitutional court.
“It is for the Polish authorities to ensure that the Constitutional Tribunal can function in accordance with the Polish constitution and in respect of the relevant case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union,” a Commission spokesperson told Euronews.
“The appointment of eight new members of the Constitutional Tribunal lies within the constitutional power of the Sejm, Poland’s parliament,” they added.

sources.headline: Explainer-What's behind Poland's constitutional crisis?
sources.text: WARSAW, Nov 2 - A crisis over the appointment of judges to Poland's Constitutional Tribunal over the weekend has pushed a simmering conflict between the country's nationalist president and the pro-European government into open confrontation.How it plays out over the coming days or weeks could have a significant impact on next year's parliamentary election and potentially push Poland closer to US President Donald Trump and away from the European mainstream.Tensions came to a head last week when the president of the Constitutional Tribunal, allied with President Karol Nawrocki's nationalists, was suspended and crowds gathered outside the court in support of him.HOW DID IT START?The dispute dates back to 2015, when the then-ruling nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) party sought to appoint Constitutional Tribunal judges to seats already filled by the previous government.Its nominees gained a majority, while critics at home and abroad argued that the court no longer met the standards of an independent and impartial tribunal established by law.After Prime Minister Donald Tusk's coalition took office in 2023, it pledged to restore the rule of law and reform the court. However, Nawrocki, a PiS ally who was elected president in 2025, has blocked some of those efforts.Earlier this year, Nawrocki refused to swear in several judges nominated by the parliamentary majority, while Constitutional Tribunal President Bogdan Swieczkowski denied the new judges access to the court.WHAT HAPPENED LAST WEEK?While heading to Africa on an official visit last Friday, Nawrocki suddenly decided to reverse course and fly home after a statement appeared on the tribunal's website saying its longest-serving judge, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, had suspended Swieczkowski and had taken charge.Police have been guarding the court since Friday afternoon, while several hundred protesters have demanded Swieczkowski's reinstatement.Once back in Warsaw, Nawrocki met senior judges overnight and political leaders on Saturday, accusing the government of staging a forced takeover of the tribunal.Tusk said in a televised address on Saturday that the court would now function independently and in line with Poland's constitution.WHAT COULD HAPPEN NEXT?A general assembly of Constitutional Tribunal judges chaired by Korwin-Piotrowska is scheduled for Tuesday, but its ability to make decisions will depend on securing a quorum of 10 of the court's 15 judges.The latest events took place a year before Poland's next parliamentary election, when Tusk's pro-European coalition will face several hard-right parties who support the president's position.Some political observers say any further escalation could galvanise voters on both sides ahead of the vote.But the conflict over the tribunal has also shown the fragmented hard-right section of the political spectrum coming together, increasing the election challenge for Tusk."It's not a conflict about the tribunal, everything is at stake," political scientist Anna Materska-Sosnowska from Warsaw University said.WHAT DOES IT MEAN FOR POLAND'S TIES WITH THE EU AND THE US?Tusk's Civic Coalition party is ahead in polls but may struggle to form a ruling majority.Poland would likely shift closer to the Trump administration if Tusk loses power next year, as the country's hard right shares many of the US president's conservative values.The US ambassador in Warsaw, Tom Rose, a Trump appointee, said on X it was not his place to interfere in Poland's internal affairs but expressed concern for its stability, security and democratic future.The European Commission said on Saturday it was closely monitoring developments and that Polish authorities must ensure the tribunal can function in accordance with the constitution and EU law.The EU withheld billions of euros in funds to Poland during the nationalist PiS-led governments of 2015 to 2023, saying their judiciary reforms had subverted democratic checks and balances.Relations with the Tusk administration have been much smoother and the flow of funds to Poland resumed.A prolonged dispute could raise institutional risks and weigh on assessments of Poland's creditworthiness, economists at Polish bank PKO BP said in a report on Monday.Rating agencies have previously said the political gridlock between Tusk and Nawrocki on a range of issues was hurting Poland's credit profile. REUTERS

sources.headline: Tusk defends overhaul of Poland’s constitutional court despite protests
sources.text: Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, has vowed to see through a contested overhaul of the country’s constitutional court, declaring that “in certain matters, there can be no compromise”.In a prime-time television address on Saturday night, Tusk was defiant, despite overnight protests that saw riot police drafted to protect the court’s building, saying the shake-up was vital to restore a tribunal crippled by years of political disputes.Paralysed for more than a decade, the court sat at the core of rule of law clashes between the rightwing Law and Justice (PiS) party and the EU during the party’s eight-year rule.Since returning to office in 2023, the centre-right Tusk has sought to unwind those judicial changes, but his agenda has been frustrated by opposition-aligned presidents with extensive veto powers. Earlier this year, president Karol Nawrocki refused to swear in five judges approved by parliament.The crisis flared again on Friday when a group of government-backed judges attempted to seize procedural control of the tribunal, suspending the PiS-appointed chief judge and deputy and prompting street protests.Conservative supporters assemble outside the constitutional court in Warsaw. Photograph: Agata Grzybowska/Anadolu/Getty ImagesDefending the action, Tusk said “there was never any doubt that the court in the form imposed by PiS was not a genuine court”, citing adverse rulings from European tribunals.He compared the opposition outrage to “a thief snatching an elderly woman’s handbag, running off, and when he is caught, he screams that he is subjected to violence”.Tusk said: “Let’s call things for what they are: for years, there have been organisations and politicians in Poland who seek to destroy democracy and the rule of law. It is no coincidence they find support among pro-Russian forces globally.”He later highlighted that Russia’s former president Dmitry Medvedev had joined the opposition in an outcry over the changes, accusing Warsaw of “a constitutional coup” and “hounding the conservatives”. “And everything is clear,” Tusk said.He also criticised opposition-aligned Nawrocki for joining the protests on Friday night and forcing his entry into the court’s building to intervene. “In a democratic state, no politician can enter a court to issue orders or intimidate judges – not even the president,” Tusk said. “We Poles have succeeded too well in building a strong state to surrender now.”He said it was the government’s duty to ensure its security and the conditions necessary for the court to operate. “And I intend to fulfil that duty,” he said.On Saturday, the European Commission urged Nawrocki to approve the new judges who were nominated by parliament, so the court could function in line with the constitution and EU law.A spokesperson for the commission said its executive was “following closely” the events in Poland.skip past newsletter promotionafter newsletter promotion“It is for the Polish authorities to ensure that the constitutional tribunal can function in accordance with the Polish constitution and in respect of the relevant case law of the court of justice of the European Union,” the spokesperson said, appearing to ally the bloc with the Polish government.However, the spokesperson also highlighted that the European court of human rights issued an interim finding in May that obliged Polish authorities to “refrain from hindering the taking up and exercise of judicial duties” by judges who are still waiting to be sworn in.The confrontation sets the battle lines before next year’s parliamentary election, with polls pointing to a close race between Tusk’s broad coalition and the nationalist right.However, experts remain divided over whether the government’s procedural gambit at the court is lawful.Poland’s Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights said on Saturday the legal basis for the temporary suspension was “questionable”, warning it would “not contribute” to restoring the court.The foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, conceded that the events outside the court were “not elegant”, but insisted: “The alternative was to concede an unconstitutional transformation of Poland into a presidential republic.”Nawrocki held some cross-party political talks on Saturday, with no apparent breakthrough. His senior aide, Zbigniew Bogucki, responded to Tusk’s address, calling the prime minister “a pathological liar, who is setting Poland ablaze”.

Poland’s constitutional crisis deepened on Saturday as the European Commission urged President Karol Nawrocki to recognise new judges appointed by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. The standoff comes ahead of next year’s parliamentary election, with polls suggesting a close race between Tusk’s coalition and the nationalist right. Camille Corcoran reports.

sources.headline: Poland’s top court turns into battleground as Tusk and pro-Trump president clash
sources.text: File photo: Demonstrators attend a protest outside the premises of Poland's Constitutional Tribunal, after the tribunal said on its website that the tribunal's president Bogdan Swieczkowski, who was a deputy justice minister under the PiS government, had been suspendedPoland’s long-running battle over judicial independence has escalated into a confrontation between prime minister Donald Tusk and president Karol Nawrocki, after the suspension of the Constitutional Tribunal’s leadership triggered protests and a police deployment outside the court in Warsaw.The latest flashpoint came on Friday, when Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska announced the one-month suspension of Tribunal president Bogdan Święczkowski and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, and said she would take charge of the institution. The move followed a dispute over the appointment of new judges, whom Święczkowski had refused to allow to take their seats.Nawrocki, an ally of the nationalist Law and Justice party (PiS) and a vocal supporter of US President Donald Trump, abandoned a visit to Senegal and returned to Warsaw. He described the suspension of the Tribunal’s leadership as a “forcible takeover of a constitutional institution”. PiS leaders also condemned the move, accusing Tusk’s government of attempting a coup.Police were deployed outside the court as hundreds of protesters gathered. Officers said their presence followed concerns about possible threats to judges and staff and risks to public order. Police also reported three arrests after people tried to enter the court complex.Tusk defended his government’s actions, saying it was seeking to restore the rule of law after years of political interference in the judiciary under PiS, which governed Poland for eight years until 2023.“This process is difficult, at times even painful, and requires decisive action. There is no other way,” Tusk said in a post on X on Saturday. In a televised address, he said that “shouting, lies, and brawling cannot be the source of law in Poland”.A decade-long dispute over the judiciaryThe Constitutional Tribunal rules on whether legislation complies with Poland’s constitution, giving control over its composition significant political and legal consequences.The current dispute has roots in 2015, when PiS came to power and challenged judicial appointments made by the outgoing government. Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal subsequently found that only three of five appointments made by the outgoing parliament had a valid legal basis. The incoming PiS majority appointed replacements, including for seats that had already been lawfully filled, while then-president Andrzej Duda refused to swear in the three validly elected judges.During its eight years in office, PiS introduced wider judicial changes that critics said increased political influence over the courts. In 2021, the European Commission warned that the party’s actions posed a “systemic risk to the rule of law in Poland” and froze EU funding over concerns about judicial independence.The European Court of Human Rights ruled in 2021 that the participation of an improperly appointed judge had deprived a company of its right to a tribunal established by law. In December 2025, the European Union’s top court also ruled that Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal did not meet the requirements of an independent court.Tusk returned to office in December 2023 promising to restore judicial independence. But efforts to reverse the changes have been complicated by the continued presence of PiS-appointed judges and Nawrocki’s role in the appointment process.This year, parliament elected eight judges to the Tribunal’s 15-member bench. Nawrocki administered the oath to three but withheld it from five others, who took their oaths without his presence. Święczkowski subsequently refused to allow the five to begin their work.The latest confrontation followed the appointment of Maciej Berek, a former minister in Tusk’s cabinet, who was prevented from taking his seat last week. The choice has also drawn criticism from within the governing camp, with some questioning whether appointing a former government minister is consistent with promises to depoliticise the judiciary.Legal experts have raised questions about the latest intervention, too. Korwin-Piotrowska’s authority to suspend the Tribunal’s president and deputy has been disputed, with her claim based on her length of service as a judge overall rather than seniority within the Tribunal.A standoff with no clear resolutionThe confrontation has exposed a difficult question for Tusk’s government: how to restore the Tribunal’s independence without creating new doubts about the legality of its actions.Marcin Matczak, a Polish lawyer, told Al Jazeera that PiS was seeking to retain control of what he described as its remaining institutional stronghold, while the government wanted to restore balance to the Tribunal. He warned that the use of police in a dispute involving the court could set a precedent for future governments.The US ambassador to Poland, Tom Rose, urged all sides to avoid escalation, warning that large crowds outside the Tribunal could make an already dangerous situation more combustible.The standoff comes as Poland faces security concerns linked to Russia’s war in neighbouring Ukraine and sabotage attacks that Tusk has attributed to Moscow. Tusk has accused his opponents of finding support among pro-Russian forces, an allegation that further sharpens the political divide.With parliamentary elections due next year, the dispute over the Tribunal is likely to remain central to the debate over Poland’s political direction and its relationship with the European Union.
